Algomancy Comprehensive Rules

Unofficial. Generated from this project's digital client. First generation (draft), effective 2026-10-10, engine at 76d01fa.

Introduction

This document is UNOFFICIAL. It describes this digital client's implementation of Algomancy, not Caleb Gannon's game. Where it and the published Manual disagree, the Manual is the game and this document is our client. The card text and rules text it quotes are Caleb Gannon's, used with permission on the terms in data/NOTICE.md.

Edition: First generation (draft). Effective 2026-10-10. Engine at commit 76d01fa.

How to read a rule

Under each rule are only its words, its examples and two warnings: "engine differs" and Untested. Everything else, its provenance, is folded under the rule as "Sources and verification" in the HTML edition and on the review page, and is the small line beneath it in the .md and .txt editions: the sources that state the rule, the tests bound to it, and the two marks below. Each rule carries a basis, the strongest kind of source that actually states it. A Printed rule is stated by the Manual, the 2023 Rulebook or a card's printed text, read literally; a Designer rule by Caleb Gannon's own answer in the rules-questions threads; a Mixed rule by more than one kind of source together. An Owner call rule is a ruling by this project's owner, with no designer source: it is the client's law, and it may not be the game's. An Engine only rule is stated by no source; it is what the engine does, and it is listed in Annex P to await the owner's sign-off.

Our own glossary is quoted where it helps, and is never counted as a source.

Where a ruling and the engine disagree, the rule states the ruling and says "engine differs", with a link to the finding. The engine is the one that is wrong, and the finding is filed as a bug.

Each rule's provenance also says what an independent verifier found when it checked the rule against the engine and its tests: Confirmed, or Partial when it could not confirm all of it, with the verifier's note. A rule that is not confirmed shows its verdict on the fold itself. Beside the verdict are the round it was verified in, how many tests the verifier ran, and how many gate test files are bound to the rule through its examples or its sources. A gate test is part of the client's test suite and runs on every check, so it keeps demonstrating the rule after verification is over. A rule that no executed test demonstrates is marked Untested.

Examples are not rules

An example illustrates the rule above it: an illustration, never a rule in its own right, and where it seems to say more than the rule, the rule wins. Most examples are bound to a test that was run and asserts them; the test is named in the rule's provenance. Some rules are demonstrated by a test with no example in words; that test is named there too.

How numbering works

Rules are numbered in three levels: section 608, rule 608.2, subrule 608.2b. Subrule letters skip l and o. A number, once published, never moves and is never reused. A new rule goes to the end of its section, even when it would read better earlier. A removed rule keeps its number and reads "[Removed: …]". Section 802 has one rule per attribute, in the engine's own order.

1. Game Concepts

100. General

100.1. In Algomancy, each player's goal is to eliminate all of their opponents. A player is eliminated by bringing their life total to 0. See rule 104.

101. Golden Rules

101.1. Printed text beats the general rules and the engine's defaults. Where a card's printed text says something different from a general rule or a default, the card is followed, unless the designer has stated a different intent for that card (rule 101.2). See rules 400.4b, 101.2.

101.5. An effect that cannot do everything it says does as much as it can. A part of an effect that cannot happen does not stop the other parts from happening. This does not make half of an action happen: a fight or an exchange that has lost one of its two units does not happen at all (704). See rule 704.

Example: Recall: "Each player recalls a unit and loses 2 life." A player with no unit to recall still loses 2 life.

Example: Amphivore carries two grafts, Flame Juggle and Ralph, and its ability runs three times. The first pass gives Amphivore to the opponent and makes three 1/1s; later passes cannot give it again, so their "If you do" makes nothing, but Flame Juggle still happens all three times.

101.6. Every effect is specific to the region it happens in. It never affects anything in another region, and it treats the players and cards in other regions as if they do not exist. A card that says "all" or "each" means all or each in this region. See rule 601.

Example: Cosmic Reversal, cast in one region, leaves a spell unit in another region alone.

Example: Molten Riftbreaker dies in its controller's home region while a battle goes on elsewhere. Its "negate all allied spells" does not reach the spell on the battle region's stack.

102.4. A card's owner is the player whose card it is. Taking control of a card does not change its owner, and neither does moving it into or out of a player's hand, bin or cache, even another player's. A card that goes into a shared zone (a draft pack, a deck or the recycle pile) leaves its ownership behind there: whoever next takes it out owns it. See rules 400.4a, 400.4c. engine differs, see F-U01-6

Example: A unit whose control has been taken is recalled: the player it was stolen from is still the card's owner.

Example: The same recalled unit goes to the hand of the player who controls it, not its owner's hand.

Example: A stolen unit is recalled to the hand of the player who stole it and played again from there. Its owner is still the player it was stolen from.

Example: A stolen card in the thief's hand is recycled. Its ownership stays behind in the recycle pile, and the player who next takes it out owns it.

104. Ending the Game

104.1. A player whose life total reaches 0 is eliminated. See rule 112.

Example: Haunting Memories sets a player's life total to twice the number of cards in all bins. With every bin empty that is 0, and that player loses.

Example: A player at 3 life takes combat damage from an unblocked attacker and the game is over.

107. Numbers, X and Symbols

107.1. X stands for a number that the card defines. An X in a mana cost is chosen by the player who plays the card. A token's X is set by the card that created it. Other cards define X with a "where X is …" clause. See rules 702, 304.

Example: Wildfire asks its caster for X; Self-Assembly with three metal makes a Robot 3.

108.2a For card text, a token is not a card: text that refers to a "card" does not include a token, even though a unit token is a unit and a spell token is a spell. The printed rules call tokens "temporary cards" to describe them to players; that does not make a token a card. See rule 702.

Example: A player casts a Fireball token in battle. That is playing a spell, so abilities that watch for a spell being played see it; it is not playing a card, so abilities that watch for a card being played do not.

110. Targets

110.1. A target is something a card or ability chooses, with the word "target", to receive its actions. The targets are selected as the card is played. See rule 702.

Example: Fight ("Target ally and another target unit fight") takes both units as targets as it is played.

Sources and verification
PrintedConfirmedverified in round 1 · verifier ran 1 test, passed · 2 gate test files
  • Printed Manual p.13: Targets: If the card mentions targets, these are
  • Printed Manual p.13: recipients for certain actions of the card. The targets
  • Printed Manual p.13: must be selected as the card is being played.
  • Tests 16-earth-a.test.ts, 49-playtest-round6.test.ts
  • Example test 16-earth-a.test.ts::Fight: BOTH units are cast-time targets, ally first
  • Key concepts.targets.what

110.1a Targets are chosen as the effect is put on the stack: when a card is played, when an ability is activated, and when a triggered ability is put on the stack. Every target of the effect is chosen then. See rules 702, 703.

Example: Plodding Pebble carries a grafted Leaping Lillik ("Delete target unit"). A Fireball damages the Pebble: as the trigger goes on the stack, the delete's target is chosen. With no enemy in the region, it must be one of your own units.

  • Designer RAQ 1355115946032889914#15: player must at that time delcare targets for all things

110.1b Each "target" in an effect's text is a separate target. An effect that says "target" twice chooses two targets.

Example: Squish chooses two targets as it is played: an ally and another unit.

110.1c "Up to N target" lets the player choose any number of targets from none to N, and "any number of target" lets the player choose none as well. Only such words make a target optional: without them every target is required (see rule 110.7).

Example: Twin Flame ("up to two target units") can be played with no targets.

Example: Tilling the Graves ("Recall two target units in your bin") says no "up to": once cast, it asks for both units and offers no way to stop at one.

Example: Penance ("Any number of target players each lose 1 life. Draw a card.") may be played with no target, and its caster still draws.

110.7. A card or ability that needs targets can be played only if every target it requires can be chosen at the same time, each one legal and different from the others. Every target a card names is required unless the card says "up to" or "any number" (see rule 110.1c). A card that targets nothing has no such requirement. See rule 702.

Example: Fight cannot be played unless its region holds an ally and another unit.

Example: Rebalance, which targets nothing, can be played with no unit of its controller's.

Example: Abduct ("Gain control of target unit with cost [x] or less …") against a lone cost-1 attacker can be played when its caster can pay an X of 1 or more. X = 0 is not offered, since at 0 there is no unit to take.

Example: Tilling the Graves ("Recall two target units in your bin") cannot be played while its caster's bin holds fewer than two units.

Example: Tidal Reversion ("For each player, recall target unit that player controls") played for free by Tides of the Cosmos takes one unit of each player, and Tides does not offer it while either player has no unit there.

110.9. An effect that changes another effect's targets must choose each new target as that target was first chosen: legal for that target's own kind and restriction, and not an object already chosen for another target of the same part of the effect. Enigmatic Warder's ability ("Change a target of target effect to me") may target only an effect that Enigmatic Warder could be a legal target of. Any other effect that changes targets may target an effect with no target that can be changed, and the change then does nothing. The client asks the player to confirm before choosing a target effect whose targets the change cannot alter. Digital client See rule 110.6.

Example: Enigmatic Warder cannot take Throw off a Cliff, which needs a unit with 4 or more defense.

110.10a A Virus being applied is an effect on the stack that targets its host. It can be redirected, an effect that answers "target effect targeting me" or an effect targeting an ally can answer it, and a unit that must be targeted if able (rule 110.12) compels it like any other targeted effect. See rule 723.

Example: Graxxlid ("Negate target effect targeting me") can negate a Virus being applied to it.

Example: Boon of Protection can negate a Virus being applied to an allied unit.

Example: With a Gatekeeper of Souls in the battle, a Virus can be applied only to the Gatekeeper.

Example: A Virus that Tides of the Cosmos plays goes onto the Gatekeeper of Souls in the battle.

110.11. An ability that triggers "when I become targeted" triggers whenever its unit is targeted, by a spell, an ability, an augment, a graft or a Virus. When the effect that targeted is put on the stack, the trigger goes on the stack above it and so resolves first. When a graft targets the unit, or an augment is applied to it in deployment, the trigger resolves first, and only then is the mod attached.

Example: Mohruung targeted by an augment makes a Crystal 2.

Example: Grafting onto Mohruung makes a Crystal 2.

Example: A spell aimed at Mohruung waits on the stack under Mohruung's trigger, so the Crystal 2 is made before the spell resolves.

Example: A graft applied to Mohruung: the Crystal 2 is made first, and the graft attaches after.

Example: An augment applied to Mohruung in deployment: the Crystal 2 is made first, then the augment attaches.

110.12. A unit that "must be targeted if able" (Gatekeeper of Souls) must be one of the targets of an effect whose targets are selected during a battle in its region, when it can legally be one. Example: In deployment, a player with a Gatekeeper of Souls in play may aim an Overbloom at another unit.

Example: During a battle in another region, a Gatekeeper of Souls at home compels nothing.

111. Costs

111.1. A cost is something a player must pay to do something: to play a card, to apply a mod, or to activate an ability. A card's mana cost, the additional costs in its brackets, and everything before the colon of an activated ability are costs. See rules 702, 705, 720.

111.1a A mana cost is paid by expending resources: each resource can be expended once per turn for 1 mana, to pay the mana cost of a card or of an ability. See rule 106.

Example: with two open resources, paying [one] for Auric Ascendant's ability and then playing Shard Sprite expends both; a second 1-cost card is not playable that turn, and both resources are open again next turn.

111.6b A player may pay N life only while they have more than N life. N is the amount the cost names; for a variable life cost it is the X chosen so far, the point being chosen included. N is not the life the payment will lose: an effect that changes how much life is lost (Arbiter of Vitality doubles it) does not change N, so the cost can still be paid, and the payment can then bring the player to 0. Without such an effect, a life cost that would bring the player to 0 cannot be paid. See rule 112.1.

Example: at exactly 9 life, Glararr's "Pay 9 life:" cannot be activated.

Example: A player with 4 life paying X life for Flesh Tithe can choose at most 3 points, and loses the 3 at once when X is set.

Example: With Arbiter of Vitality in play, a player at 15 life may pay Glararr's 9 life: they lose 18 and the game is over for them.

111.7. An activated ability's whole cost is paid when the ability is activated, before it is put on the stack. A fixed cost is paid after the ability's targets are chosen. Example: Infernal Cultivator's "Sacrifice X units:" kills the units as the ability is activated, so a negation cannot give them back.

111.8. When a triggered ability's effect says "sacrifice me. If you do, …", the sacrifice is part of the effect, not a cost: the ability goes on the stack with its source still in play, players may respond, and the source is sacrificed as the ability resolves. The sacrifice is not optional. If the source is no longer in play when the ability resolves, it cannot be sacrificed, and the "If you do" part does nothing.

Example: Eldritch Dreamtender's column deals combat damage to an opponent. Its ability goes on the stack with Dreamtender still in play; Dreamtender is sacrificed when the ability resolves, and only then is the opponent's hand looked at and a card discarded.

Example: Dreamtender is destroyed in response to its ability. When the ability resolves, nothing is sacrificed, so no hand is looked at and nothing is discarded.

111.9. A payment that an effect's text asks for while it resolves ("you may pay [one] to …", "unless its controller pays [x]") is not a cost of putting it on the stack. The ability goes on the stack without it, and the player decides whether to pay when it resolves. See rules 702.5a, 704.

111.10c A cost modifier applies to what its text names. One that names "spells" applies to every spell played, spell units and spell tokens included. One that names "cards" applies to every card played, units included, and not to spell tokens, which are not cards. Neither applies to applying a mod, which is not playing a card. 112.1. Each player begins the game with 30 life. A player whose life is reduced to 0 is eliminated. See rules 103, 104.

112.1a A life total changes only by being gained or lost. Damage dealt to a player makes that player lose that much life, and paying life is losing it. One payment, or one effect, that makes a player lose N life is one loss of N life, not N losses of 1.

Example: Throwing Boulder's 3 damage to a player is a loss of 3 life, and the [Pay 2 life] that Arbiter of Armistice adds to a card played during battle is a loss of 2 life.

Example: With Life Plant in play, paying X = 29 life for Flesh Tithe is one loss of 29 life, so Life Plant creates 29 units.

Example: Torrential Reclamation, which loses 1 life for each ally it recalls, loses it as one change, so Life Plant creates that many units.

113. Timestamps

113.1. Effects that apply to the same layer apply in timestamp order. Where they conflict, the later effect takes precedence over the earlier one. See rule 709.

Example: Monke resolves in battle, so other units lose all attributes. Afterwards a player augments Chitin Shredder, a Virus, onto their unit: that unit has Powerful, because the virus is later than Monke.

  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-10-09 — quoted from the retired ruling register: the same layer have timestamps and latter ones take precedence over former."*

  • Example test 390-raq-stack.test.ts::RAQ timestamps: a virus applied AFTER Monke still gives its attribute

113.2. An effect's timestamp is when it began to apply. A static ability's effect has the timestamp of the card that carries it, a mod's has the time it was applied, and an effect from a resolved spell or ability has the time it resolved. What a card prints is older than any effect.

Example: an attribute granted to a unit while Suppression Field is still on the stack is lost when the spell resolves; one granted after it resolves is kept.

  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-10-09 — quoted from the retired ruling register: - **What a card prints is the oldest thing on it** (`E.PRINTED`), so every stripper
  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-10-09 — quoted from the retired ruling register: Attributes/Abilities"): *"Suppression field just removes attributes from the time

113.2a A change of control does not change an effect's timestamp. When a card, or the unit a mod is on, changes control, its effects keep the timestamps they already had, including when they now apply to other units. See rule 113.3.

Example: Transmogrifant ("[Augment] Your other units gain +2/+2 and lose all attributes and abilities.") is on Player B's The Bonesculptor. Later, Pernicious Photosynthesis gives Player A's units Piercing until regroup. Then Rebalance gives Player A The Bonesculptor, so Transmogrifant now covers Player A's other units: they lose what they print and keep the Piercing, because Transmogrifant's effect is still older than it.

113.2b In a step both players take at the same time, the haste step and deployment, the initiative player's plays are timestamped before the other player's. This client stamps them so whatever order the two players made them in, and keeps each player's own plays in the order that player made them. Digital client See rules 507.3, 507.3a.

Example: In one deployment the non-initiative player casts Pernicious Photosynthesis first and the initiative player then augments Transmogrifant onto The Bonesculptor. Transmogrifant is the older. When Rebalance later gives the non-initiative player The Bonesculptor, their units keep the Piercing.

Example: With the same plays in the same order and the initiative the other way round, Pernicious Photosynthesis is the older, and the units lose the Piercing.

2. Parts of a Card

200. General

200.1. An Algomancy card can show these parts: a name, a mana cost, an affinity requirement, a timing icon, stats (power and defense), a type line of types and attributes, abilities, and a set symbol. Every card has a name; the other parts appear only on the cards that need them. Some cards also print an alternative-cost banner (203) or an augment symbol (208). See rules 201, 202, 203, 204, 205, 206, 207, 208, 209. Untested

  • Printed Rulebook 2023 p.3: ▪ Most cards have Abilities (7), which describe the card’s effects.

202. Cost Orb and Pips

202.1. The cost orb shows the card's mana cost: the number of resources a player must expend to play it. See rules 106, 111.

Example: Good Whale (cost orb 6) cannot be played with five resources; played with seven, it expends six and leaves one open.

202.2. The pips with the cost are the card's affinity requirement. To play the card, its controller must have at least that many resources of each pip's element among their resources. The requirement is met, not paid: expended resources count toward it. See rule 105.

Example: Two wood resources and any number of shards can pay for many [gg] cards in one turn.

205.4. On a graft card the graft symbol divides an ability into a cause, before the symbol, and an effect, after it. When the card is grafted onto another, only the text after its graft symbol is added. See rule 722.

206. Power and Defense

206.1. A unit's stats are two numbers, printed power/defense. Power is how much damage the unit deals in combat. Defense is how much damage it can take before it dies. See rules 112, 608, 713.

Example: An unblocked Rune Channeler (4/3) deals 4 damage; a Good Whale (7/5) survives 4 damage and dies to a fifth.

  • Printed Manual p.12: Denote the power and defense

  • Key card.stats.what

206.2. Stats mark a card as a unit. A spell has no stats, and neither does a spell token. Spell units do have stats, and enter play as units with them when they resolve. See rules 301, 303.

Example: Lonely Forager, a Spell Unit, resolves into play as a 3/1 unit; Resurrect, a plain spell, goes to the bin.

Example: No spell in the card pool carries a power or a defense.

Example: A Fireball spell token carries no stats.

206.4. A unit's stats are worked out in six layers, applied in this order: 1. printed stats, as shown on the card; 2. base stats, which effects can set to something other than the printed stats; 3. stat changes, such as temporary bonuses and +1/+1 or -1/-1 counters; 4. attributes, such as Tough; 5. Inverted; 6. Unaware. See rules 709, 802.

Example: A 0/4 Tough unit with a +1/+1 counter is a 1/10: the counter (layer 3) applies before Tough doubles defense (layer 4).

300. General

301.8a Those counters are put on the unit as it enters, by the player who spawns it. So an ability that triggers when a player puts counters on a unit triggers, and an effect that changes how many counters would be put on a unit changes them. See rules 708, 112.

Example: A Robot 2 created by Living Forge counts as "you put counters on an ally": its controller's Scrapyard Custodian draws a card.

Example: Aethercap Siphoner arriving with its counters also counts as "you put counters on an ally".

Example: With an allied Flux Resonator, Powerforge Synergist enters with three +1/+1 counters instead of two.

Example: The units Wake the Dead plays out of a bin are played: Bloomcaster and Stalwart Sentinel both see them.

Example: The unit Gridxlan lets its player play from the bin is played: it is paid for, and only one is allowed each deployment.

Example: A played Jelly is a played spell, gives the target -2/-2, and then its body is a 2/1 unit in play.

303.5. Playing a spell unit is playing a spell, and while it is on the stack it is a spell: anything that refers to a spell, or to an allied spell, applies to it. See rules 300.5a, 701.

304.10. A token that leaves play goes to the zone it was sent to: a unit token that dies enters the bin, and a recalled token, unit or spell, enters its controller's hand. It really is there, so abilities that watch that zone see it. It is then erased from the game, before anything that triggered on its arrival resolves. See rules 410, 713, 405, 402.

Example: A unit token that dies enters the bin, is not trashed, and is then erased.

Example: Rider of the Tides, which watches cards entering a hand during battle, sees a recalled unit token.

Example: A Fireball recalled off the stack enters its controller's hand, Rider of the Tides sees it, and it is erased.

305. Modifications

305.1. A modification (mod) is a card that is applied to another card instead of being played. A modified card is treated as a single card with all of the text its mods add, except that a spell or a spell token that is modified gains only the mod's attributes (721). The two kinds of modification are augment and graft. See rules 720, 721, 722, 723, 724.

Example: Curio Drifter augmented onto a Good Whale is not played and gives the Whale Evasive; Biotoxicity is grafted; a Fireball augmented with Bloomcaster does not create 1/1s.

4. Zones

400. General

400.1. The zones of the game are the deck, the hand, the cache, play, the bin, the stack, the erased pile, the recycle pile and the pack. See rules 401, 402, 403, 404, 405, 406, 407, 408, 409.

Sources and verification

  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-08-25 — quoted from the retired ruling register: The ACTIVE ZONES are PLAY (the field / a formation) and the STACK.
  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-09-16 — quoted from the retired ruling register: **past the mark**, into the recycle pile, not onto the bottom of the live deck.
  • Tests 418-cr-zones.test.ts
  • Demonstrated by test 418-cr-zones.test.ts::cr:zones.general.list — the engine keeps cards in exactly nine zones: deck, hand, cache, play, bin, stack, erased pile, recycle pile and pack
  • Key zones.general.list

400.2. Play and the stack are the active zones. The hand, the deck, the bin, the cache and the erased pile are inactive zones. See rules 404, 406, 803.

Example: A printed Unstable card is erased leaving play or the stack, and only binned leaving the hand, the deck or the cache.

400.2a Whether a zone is active matters to {Unstable}: an {Unstable} card is erased in place of entering a bin only when it leaves an active zone. A card leaving an inactive zone for a bin is binned normally, {Unstable} or not. See rules 405, 803.

Example: Aberrant Statweaver (printed {Unstable}) discarded from a hand goes to the bin and stays there: the hand is inactive.

Example: The same card negated off the stack is erased: the stack is active.

400.4. A card that leaves play for a bin, a hand, a cache or an erased pile goes to that zone of the player who controlled it when it left play, not to its owner's. See rules 102, 711.

Example: A unit stolen with a control-changing effect is recalled. It goes to the hand of the player who stole it.

Example: A stolen unit dies. It goes to its controller's bin, and its controller trashes it.

Example: A stolen unit is erased from play. It and its mods go to the erased pile of the player who stole it.

400.4a A card's owner never changes. Changing zones, changing controller and being put into play out of another player's zone all leave the card owned by the same player.

Example: Wake the Dead puts a unit from the opponent's bin into play under the caster's control; the opponent still owns it.

Example: A stolen unit that is recalled is still owned by the player it was stolen from.

406. The Stack

406.1. The stack is the zone where cards being played, and abilities, wait to resolve. The last thing put on the stack resolves first. See 703. See rules 703, 704.

When a card on the stack resolves, is negated or fails to resolve, it goes to the bin unless it enters play or something sends it elsewhere: an {Unstable} card is erased (see rule 405.5), a card whose own text erases it goes to the erased pile (see rule 406.4a), and a recall puts it into a hand. A card that goes to the bin this way is not trashed, because it comes from the stack. See rules 704, 405.4, 405.5, 406.4a.

407.3. A token is never recorded on the erased pile, because a token is not a card and the erased pile is a list of cards. See rule 410.5.

Example: A unit token sent to the cache ceases to exist there and is not recorded on the erased pile.

Example: A token unit carrying a real mod is erased from play. The mod is recorded on the erased pile; the token is not.

Example: A spell token recalled off the stack is not recorded on the erased pile.

Example: A token that dies enters the bin, is not trashed, and then ceases to exist, without being recorded.

408.2b When anything that uses the deck needs a card past the mark, whatever the reason, the recycle pile is shuffled and put above the mark, under the cards still left in the deck; the mark goes back to the very bottom, with an empty recycle pile behind it. Taking the last card above the mark does not by itself reshuffle the pile: it is shuffled only when a card past the mark is needed. An effect that reveals more cards than are above the mark reshuffles when it reaches the mark and keeps revealing until it has its full number. See rule 401.4.

410. Zone Changes

410.1. A card that leaves play and comes back is a new object. It does not remember its earlier time in play.

Example: Engorged Caudex is recalled and played again; its once-per-turn grafted draw works again the same turn.

Sources and verification
DesignerConfirmedverified in round 1 · verifier ran 1 test, passed · 1 gate test file
  • Designer RAQ 1355115946032889914#16: A unit that leaves play and comes back is a new object
  • Designer RAQ 1355115946032889914#16: calebgannon: "Yes that works"
  • Tests 393-raq-mods.test.ts
  • Example test 393-raq-mods.test.ts::RAQ Graft 101 calebgannon: a recalled and replayed Engorged Caudex is a new object
  • Key zones.changes.new-object

410.1a An effect aimed at a card that has since changed zones does not affect it. An effect aimed at a card that is still in the same zone affects it only if the card is still a legal target for the slot it was chosen for; otherwise that target is lost as well. If every target is lost, the effect fails to resolve. See rules 704, 110.

Example: An opponent's Luminous Arc is aimed at one of your units; you answer with Organic Exchange on two of your own units. They are still in play, so the Luminous Arc still resolves.

Example: An opponent ambushes with Orblish Horroth to recall target ally; you take control of that unit in response. It is no longer their ally, so nothing is recalled.

Example: Minor Kraken's target grows past 5 defense before it resolves, and is not recalled.

410.7. When a unit leaves play for a bin, it dies (or, if it was exchanged out of play, despawns) before anything is trashed. The unit and its mods leave play; then its death or despawn happens, and the abilities that trigger on it trigger; only then is any card trashed (see rule 801.2).

Example: A unit with no mods dies and goes to its controller's bin. Its death comes first, then it is trashed.

Example: Hooba-Mon exchanges itself for a unit card in its controller's bin. It despawns, and only then is it trashed. It does not die.

5. Turn Structure

500. General

500.1. A turn has four phases, in this order: the planning phase, the battle phase, the regroup phase and the deployment phase. See rules 501, 505, 506, 507.

500.2. Turns are global: all players share the same phases and sync up at the end of each step. In a 1v1 or team game, the printed rules take some steps in initiative order: the initiative player, or team, acts first, and the non-initiative player waits to see what they did before acting (see rule 501.4 and rule 507.3). 503.4. In constructed there are no packs. In the draft step each player draws 2 more cards from their own deck and then recycles 2 cards from their hand. Since this comes straight after the draw step, the two are taken together: draw 4, then recycle 2. See rules 408, 901.

505. Battle Phase

505.1. The battle phase is the only interactive phase of the game. In it players manage their units across the regions: they attack into other regions or keep units back to defend. See rules 601, 604.

Example: Player A attacks with a Good Whale: the Whale moves into Player B's region, and Player A enters that region too.

505.3a Round 1 runs in this order: (1) the initiative team declares its attacks, sending units into non-initiative regions; (2) a priority window; (3) the non-initiative team declares its blocking formations and may at the same time send units out to counterattack; (4) a priority window; (5) the combat step, in which all units in formation deal combat damage at the same time; (6) the after-combat step, the last priority window in that region. See rules 604, 605, 606, 607, 608, 609, 610.

6. Regions, Formations and Battle

600. General

600.1. Units are the basis of combat. They attack opponents, enter other players' regions and defend against units that enter their own. Combat takes place inside regions (rule 601), with the units that take part arranged in formations (rule 602) made up of columns (rule 603). See rules 601, 602, 603.

Example: Two units attack into the opponent's region. The defender blocks one of them; the other is unblocked and deals its damage to the defending player.

Sources and verification

  • Printed Rulebook 2023 p.10: Units are the basis of combat, as they are used to attack opponents, enter new regions and defend yourself against invaders.
  • Tests 421-cr-regions-formations.test.ts
  • Example test 421-cr-regions-formations.test.ts::cr:combat.general.units — an attacking unit enters the defending player region, an unblocked attacker damages that player, and a defending unit blocks an attacker

601. Regions

601.1. All gameplay takes place inside regions. There is one region for each player, and each player starts in their own region.

Sources and verification

601.1a Each region is isolated from every other region. Nothing in one region interacts with anything in another region, and each region treats the players and cards in other regions as if they don't exist. See rule 601.8.

Example: Towering Colossus prints “Enemies gain +2/+2.” An enemy unit standing in a different region from the Colossus does not get the bonus.

601.2a The stack, the bins, the hands and the caches are bound by the regional rule like everything else (rule 101.6). Each region has its own stack. No player owns it: it is shared by the players present in that region, and only they can put effects on it or respond to them. A player's bin, hand and cache are tied to that player: an effect can affect them only in a region where that player is present (rule 601.4c). See rule 601.4c.

Example: During deployment, an effect that targets a cached card can reach only its controller's own cache. In battle, where both players are present, it can reach either cache.

Example: Molten Riftbreaker dies in its controller's home region during a battle elsewhere: its "negate all allied spells" leaves the spell on the battle region's stack alone. Dying in the battle region, it negates it.

601.6. Battle is resolved one region at a time. Once players have begun interacting inside a region, every step of battle is completed in that region before those players can interact anywhere else. See rules 505, 610.

602. Formations

602.1. When units attack or block, they are placed in a formation. The units a player attacks with make up that player's attacking formation; the units a player blocks with make up that player's defending formation. See rules 604, 606.

Example: A player attacks with three units in two columns; those three units are the attacking formation. The two units the defender blocks with are the defending formation.

602.1a A formation has a front row and a back row, and any number of columns. Each column of a formation holds at most two units: one in the front row and one in the back row. See rule 603.1.

Example: A player may attack five columns wide, but cannot put three units in one column.

602.1b An attacking formation is set during the attack step. A defending formation is set during the block step. See rules 604, 606.

603. Columns, Adjacency and Edges

603.1. A column is one file of the battle line: the attacking units in it and the defending units placed in front of it. Each side of a column holds at most two units. A defending unit placed in front of an attacking column blocks that whole column. See rules 602.1a, 606, 608.1c.

Example: One unit blocks a column of two attackers. Neither attacker deals damage to the defending player.

  • Tests 421-cr-regions-formations.test.ts

603.1a Combat attributes are shared by the units in the same column of a formation, and are not shared with units to their left or right (see rule 802.1). See rules 802.1, 712.

Example: A unit with Flying attacks in the front of a column. The unit behind it has Flying too; the unit in the next column does not.

603.1b A defending unit may also block in a column where there is no attacker (a side-block). Side-block columns stand beside the attacking line, on either side of it (see rule 606). Any number of units may side-block, and each may stand in a column of its own. See rule 606.

Example: Two defending units block where no attacker is, each in its own column beside the attack.

Example: A single 2/5 attacks; the defender side-blocks to its left with a 1/1. The 1/1 stands in a new column left of the attack, the attacking column stays unblocked, and it deals 2 to the defender.

603.2. A unit in a formation is adjacent to its left, right, front and back neighbours in that formation.

Example: Inspiration gives +2/+2 to its controller's units adjacent to it in formation, and to no others.

603.2a A unit in a formation has at most three adjacent positions: the same row of the column to its left, the same row of the column to its right, and the other slot of its own column. The other row of a neighbouring column is diagonal, and is not adjacent. Where a line ends, there is a position past the end only as rule 603.3 allows. See rule 603.3.

Example: Hooba-Nan stands in the front row of a middle column. Its adjacent slots are the front rows of the columns on either side and the slot behind it, and nothing diagonal.

Example: A blocker stands next to an unblocked attacking column. It has no adjacent position in that column.

604. Attacking

604.1. Attacking is how a player brings units, and the spell tokens that travel with them, into a neighbouring enemy region for battle. Attacks are declared in the attack step, the first step of a battle round (see 505). See rules 505, 601.

Example: The initiative player declares an attack with one unit. That unit moves into the other player's region, and at regroup it returns home.

606. Blocking

606.1. Blocking is how a player who has been attacked defends. In the block step, the defending player may place its units in front of the attacking formation. See rules 602, 608.

Example: Two columns attack, a 3/5 and a 4/5; the defending player places a 2/5 in front of the 3/5. That column is blocked and the two units deal damage to each other; the unblocked 4/5 hits the player.

606.2c These attributes change which units may block a column, or how many it takes: Flying (802.2), Feeble (802.12), Evasive (802.13), Sneaky (802.14), Alluring (802.15) and Pure (802.25). See rules 802.2, 802.12, 802.13, 802.14, 802.15, 802.25.

Example: Wisps are Feeble and cannot block.

Example: Curio Drifter is Evasive, so its column needs two blockers.

608. Combat Damage Step

608.1. The combat damage step is the step of a battle in which the units in formation deal combat damage. It begins once blocks have been declared and all players have passed priority in the window that follows them, and it is followed by the after combat step (see rule 609). See rules 607, 609.

Example: A 2/5 attacks and is blocked by a 2/5. After blocks, the block window opens; once both players pass, each deals 2 to the other, and then the after combat step begins.

608.1a The combat damage step takes place separately in each region where a battle takes place. A region that was not attacked has no combat damage step. See rules 601, 609.

Example: The first attacker declares no attack, so the defending player's region has no combat damage step. The second player then attacks, and the only combat damage step of the turn is in the first player's region.

608.1c Combat damage is dealt by columns. The attacking units of one column deal their combat damage together, as one source, and so do the blocking units of one column. In this section, each of these two groups is called a half-column: a column has an attacking half and a blocking half. See rules 603, 802.20.

Example: Two Slinks (Thieving) attack in one column and are not blocked. The column is one source of combat damage, so its controller draws one card, not two.

608.2. The combat damage step has three damage sub-steps, taken in this order: the Swift sub-step, the normal sub-step and the Sluggish sub-step. Each half-column strikes (deals its combat damage) only in the sub-steps that rule 608.2a gives it. The two halves of one column are scheduled separately. See rules 802.4, 802.5.

Example: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) is blocked by a 1/5, and Ambling Mountaintop (Sluggish) attacks unblocked. The Drifter deals 2 in the Swift sub-step, the 1/5 strikes back in the normal sub-step and kills it, and the Mountaintop deals its damage last.

Example: Dune Drifter (Swift) and Lithoghul attack in one column, so Lithoghul would strike in the Swift sub-step. If Dune Drifter is recalled, Lithoghul at once strikes in the normal sub-step instead.

608.2e A half-column that has struck in the Swift sub-step does not strike in the normal sub-step, even if the unit that gave it Swift has since left the column, and even if a new unit has since been put into that column. A half-column that has struck in the normal sub-step does not strike in the Sluggish sub-step, even if it has since gained Sluggish. A half-column that struck in the Swift sub-step and has Sluggish in the Sluggish sub-step strikes again then (rule 608.2c). This record belongs to the half-column, not to the units in it, and it stays with that column if the columns are renumbered (for example, when a new column is opened to its left). See rule 603.

Example: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) and a 3/3 attack in one column; a 1/1 attacks in another. The Swift column deals 5 in the Swift sub-step. Dune Drifter is then recalled. In the normal sub-step only the 1/1's column strikes.

Example: After Dune Drifter's column strikes in the Swift sub-step, Dune Drifter is recalled and Tiderunner Initiate is played into the emptied column. Tiderunner Initiate deals no normal combat damage.

608.3b In a split step, each sub-step that was scheduled, when the step began, to have a half-column strike in it is a separate step. After each such sub-step except the last scheduled one, the abilities that triggered during it are put on the stack and players receive priority; the next sub-step deals no damage until that stack has resolved and all players have passed priority in succession with it empty. State-based changes (deaths, back-row units moving forward, lost shared attributes) have already happened when this window opens. See rules 703, 706.

Example: Bripp (4 power) and Bloated Manablub (2 power) attack in normal columns, and Adversary of the Deep (2/2, Sluggish; 'Whenever a player loses life, put that many +1/+1 counters on me') attacks in a third column. None are blocked. The normal sub-step deals 6; the step stops, Adversary's trigger resolves with priority, and Adversary strikes in the Sluggish sub-step for 8.

Example: At the boundary, the stack holds Adversary of the Deep's trigger. Its controller has the initiative and receives priority first; the other player may respond once they pass.

608.3c A sub-step in which no half-column was scheduled to strike when the step began is not a separate step: no window opens after it. A scheduled sub-step keeps its window even if every half-column scheduled for it has since been destroyed. No window opens after the last scheduled sub-step; a half-column that still strikes in a later sub-step (rule 608.2f) strikes without a window before it, and then the after combat step begins.

Example: Dune Drifter (Swift) and Lithoghul attack in separate columns and are not blocked. Half-columns strike in the Swift and normal sub-steps and nothing strikes in the Sluggish sub-step, so there is exactly one window, between the Swift and normal sub-steps.

Example: Dune Drifter (Swift) and a 1/1 attack in separate columns and are not blocked. At the window after the Swift sub-step, Dune Drifter's column gains Sluggish. The 1/1 strikes in the normal sub-step and no window follows; Dune Drifter's column then strikes in the Sluggish sub-step, and the after combat step begins.

608.3e Between sub-steps, the game's state is updated before anything else: units with lethal damage are destroyed, a unit behind a removed unit moves to the front row, and attributes shared by a removed unit are lost. A unit destroyed in an earlier sub-step deals no damage in a later one, and damage in a later sub-step is assigned to the formation as it then stands. Columns do not close gaps after blocks have been declared. See rules 602, 603.

Example: Dune Drifter (2/1, Swift) is blocked by a 2/2 in front of a 4/3. Its Swift damage destroys the 2/2; the 4/3 is already in front when the boundary window opens, and in the normal sub-step it destroys Dune Drifter while taking no damage.

Example: A blocking column whose attacker was destroyed in an earlier sub-step deals nothing in a later sub-step.

608.4. Each attacking half-column deals its combat damage either to the defending player or to the blocking half-column in front of it, and each blocking half-column deals its combat damage to the attacking half-column it blocks. Piercing can also carry combat damage to a player (see rule 802.16). An attacking column is blocked once a blocking unit has been placed in front of it, normally in the block step (see rule 606) or later as rule 608.4d allows. See rules 606, 802.16.

Example: A 3/5 and a 4/5 attack in two columns; a 2/5 blocks the 3/5. The 3/5 deals 3 to the blocker, the blocker deals 2 to the 3/5, and the 4/5 deals 4 to the defending player.

608.4c Once an attacking column is blocked, it remains blocked for the rest of the battle, however its blockers leave the blocking half-column: destroyed, recalled, erased or stolen. If no blocking unit remains when that column strikes, an attacking half-column without Piercing deals no combat damage at all, and one with Piercing deals all of its damage to the defending player (see rule 802.16). See rules 606, 802.16.

Example: A vanilla attacker is blocked; the blocker is then recalled before damage. The column stays blocked and the defending player is dealt no damage.

Example: A 7/5 without Piercing is blocked by a 1/1 that dies before damage. It deals nothing to the defending player.

608.8. 608.8c If combat damage that would be dealt to a player is dealt to a unit instead (as Oorblak's ability does), the replacement applies to that damage once. Without Piercing, all of that damage is dealt to the unit. With Piercing, the damage beyond the unit's lethal damage is still combat damage that would be dealt to the player: another such effect that has not applied (a second Oorblak) may take it, the same one may not, and what none takes is dealt to the player. A redirect applies before an effect that changes how combat damage is dealt to a player (Blightsea Polyp); that effect applies only to damage actually dealt to the player, such as Piercing excess no redirect took. Damage a redirect takes is not dealt to the player. If all of a column's combat damage to a player is redirected, the column has dealt that player no combat damage: Lethal kills no one, Thieving draws nothing, and nothing that triggers when a column deals combat damage to a player triggers. If some of it gets past the redirects (Piercing excess), the column has dealt the player that much. An ability that triggers when its column deals combat damage, with no player named (Vroot), does trigger on a redirected hit: the column dealt that damage to the unit that took it (see rule 608.9a). See rules 708, 802.16.

Example: 10 Piercing combat damage that would be dealt to a player is redirected into a 2/4 Oorblak. 4 destroy it, and the other 6 are dealt to the player.

Example: A non-Piercing overkill redirected into Oorblak is absorbed whole; nothing reaches the player.

Example: 10 Piercing combat damage and two 2/4 Oorblaks: 4 destroy the first, the 6 left are still combat damage and the second takes 4 of them, and 2 reach the player.

Example: With three 2/4 Oorblaks the third takes the last 2, and nothing reaches the player.

Example: Blightsea Polyp and Oorblak, in either order: Oorblak takes the column's damage, and no rot is gained. With a Piercing column, the excess past the Oorblak reaches the player and is dealt as 1 rot.

Example: Blightsea Polyp beside two Oorblaks: the player chooses only between the Oorblaks, and no rot is gained.

Example: Gublin (Lethal) attacks and all of its combat damage is redirected into Oorblak. The player is dealt nothing and lives.

Example: A wholly redirected hit raises no "deals combat damage to a player" trigger and costs the player no life.

Example: A partly redirected hit is dealt as what got past Oorblak.

Example: Vroot's 10-power Piercing column puts 4 into Oorblak and 6 past it: each opponent gains 10, all the combat damage its column dealt.

608.9. An ability that triggers on combat damage, or on something combat damage causes (such as a unit being destroyed), triggers when that event happens, during the combat damage step, and its trigger condition is checked then. It is put on the stack later, as rules 608.9b and 608.9c describe, and only then are its targets chosen. See rules 706, 703.

Example: Lithoghul attacks and is blocked by a Geode. In the damage step the Geode deals 1 to Lithoghul, and Lithoghul's 'whenever I am dealt damage' ability triggers then; nothing goes on the stack or resolves until the after combat step.

608.9a An ability that triggers 'when my column deals combat damage' triggers in each sub-step in which its own column deals combat damage, and only for damage its own column dealt; another column's damage does not trigger it. A 0-power unit with such an ability triggers if its column's combined power is greater than 0. Such an ability counts combat damage its column deals to anything: to the units blocking it, to a unit that a redirect deals the damage to instead (Oorblak), and to a player. "That much" counts all of it. See rule 706.

Example: A Swift and Sluggish column with Vroot strikes twice, and Vroot's ability triggers twice.

Example: Vroot's 'that much' is its own column's damage, not the total dealt to the player by every column.

Example: Vroot is blocked by a 0/20 unit: its column deals the blocker 4, and each opponent gains 4.

Example: Vroot's column is wholly redirected into Oorblak: the column dealt Oorblak 4, and each opponent gains 4.

608.9b In an unsplit step, every ability that triggered during the combat damage step is put on the stack in the after combat step, together with the abilities that trigger at the start of the after combat step, as one batch. The initiative player puts all of theirs on the stack first, in the order they choose, and then the other player puts theirs; each player may interleave the two kinds in any order. All players may respond to them. See rules 609, 706.

Example: One player's combat-damage trigger and after-combat trigger are put in order together, in one choice.

Example: The initiative player's triggers go on the stack first and sit at the bottom.

608.9c In a split step, the abilities that triggered during a sub-step other than the last scheduled one are put on the stack, in the same order as in rule 608.9b, at the window after that sub-step, and resolve before the next sub-step deals damage (rule 608.3b). 608.9e An ability that works only while its card is in the bin can trigger on combat damage only if the card is already in the bin when that damage is dealt. A unit destroyed by combat damage is not in the bin while that same damage is dealt, but a unit destroyed in an earlier sub-step is. See rules 405, 706.

609. After Combat

609.1. The after combat step is the last step of a battle round. It follows the combat damage step, in the region where that battle is fought, and it is the last priority window for interaction in that region before regroup. See rules 505.2, 608.

609.2. The after combat step is a priority window. The initiative player receives priority first, then priority passes to the non-initiative player in the region. When all players pass priority in succession with the stack empty, the after combat step ends. See rule 703.

Example: After combat, the initiative player passes, the non-initiative player casts a spell, and both then pass. The spell resolves and the initiative player receives priority again. When both pass with the stack empty, the step ends.

610.3. Spell tokens may go with counterattacking units, under the same conditions as with an attack (see rule 604.2c). A counterattack made only of spell tokens is not allowed: spell tokens need at least one counterattacking unit to go with. A spell token sent with a counterattack is committed as the units are: in round 2 it must ride with the counterattacking formation, with the formation as a whole rather than with any one unit. If every unit sent with it has died, it cannot ride and is not owed: it reaches no priority window, and is erased unused at regroup. See rules 604.2c, 606.5a.

Example: Three units and a Fireball token were sent. In round 2 a formation that leaves the Fireball behind is refused.

Example: The only unit sent with a Fireball token dies before round 2: no attack is possible, the battle phase ends with no window, and the token is erased at regroup.

610.4b If the first battle round had a battle, only the units sent to counterattack can attack in the second battle round, and every one of them still there and able to attack must attack. In its attack step the non-initiative team puts all of them into formation, in any shape; the shape is chosen then, not when the units are sent. Every spell token sent with them that is still there rides along too (see rule 610.3). A sent unit that died on its return is not owed. See rule 604.2f.

Example: The non-initiative player sent Conduit of Pain at block time. In round 2 it is the only unit they can attack with, and it must attack: declining is refused.

Example: Three units were sent. Declining, or leaving one off to the side, is refused; any shape that holds all three is accepted.

Example: Two units were sent and one dies on its return: the other alone is owed, and it forms by itself.

7. Spells, Abilities and Effects

700. General

700.1. An effect is anything on the stack. Whenever a card is played, or an ability is activated or triggered, it is added to the stack as an effect. A unit or spell unit on the stack is an effect too. See rule 703.

Example: a {Battle} unit being played sits on the stack and can be chosen by an effect that says "target effect" (Dematerialize).

Sources and verification
MixedConfirmedverified in round 1 · verifier ran 1 test, passed · 1 gate test file
  • Printed Manual p.28: triggered, it is added to
  • Printed Manual p.28: the stack as an “effect”.
  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-08-24 — quoted from the retired ruling register: an effect, including units and spell units. Units aren't spells, so if they say
  • Tests 118-stack-effect.test.ts
  • Example test 118-stack-effect.test.ts::CR 700.1: a unit on the stack is a legal "target effect" (Dematerialize)
  • Key effects.general.effect

700.1a A spell effect is an effect that is a spell: a spell, a spell unit or a spell token on the stack. A unit on the stack is an effect but not a spell effect, and neither is an Ambush, since the card played as an Ambush is a unit: a card that says "spell effect" cannot affect either of them.

Example: Null Drone ("target spell effect") cannot choose a plain unit on the stack, but can choose a spell unit.

Example: Dreadwave Devourer ("Negate target spell effect") cannot target an Ambush on the stack, and the Ambush resolves.

Example: A spell unit and a spell token on the stack are spell effects; an Ambush is not.

Example: Nothyr ("negate up to one target nonspell effect") can choose a {Battle} unit on the stack.

701. Playing and Applying

701.1. Only units and spells are played, whatever zone they are played from. Applying a modification is not playing a card (701.2).

Example: Godray and Monke played from hand, and Trench Stalker played from the bin, are plays; a Virus applied to the attacker is not.

701.4. A card played during the resolution of another effect is played. During battle it is put on the stack and can be responded to (rule 703.5), and abilities that trigger on a play see it. See rule 703.5.

Example: A unit Wake the Dead plays waits on the stack and can be answered; a negated one never arrives.

Example: A card an effect plays where nobody can respond is still announced as played, for a unit and for a spell.

702. Casting Spells

702.1. To play a card, a player must meet its affinity requirement, pay its mana cost, select its targets as it is played, and resolve whatever is inside its brackets (an additional cost to pay or a mode to choose). See rules 105, 110, 111.

Example: Arc Lightning (rr, cost 4) cannot be played with four water resources (no affinity) or with only two fire resources (not enough mana); with two fire and two water it can.

702.8. A card or ability that needs targets can be played only if every target it requires can be chosen at the same time, each one legal and different from the others. Every target is required unless the card says "up to" or "any number". A triggered ability's targets are required in the same way: if a legal target exists, it must take one, even one of its controller's own units. A triggered ability whose "you may" governs its target ("you may recall target ally") offers the decline at the time its targets are chosen: its controller chooses a target or declines, and a declined ability does nothing. Once it has one target, every other target it needs is required. Choosing a target is choosing to use it, so no second "you may" is asked as it resolves; a payment its text asks for is still asked then (see rule 111.9). See rule 110.

Example: Fight cannot be played unless the region holds an ally and another unit.

Example: Tidal Reversion cannot be played while one player has no unit to recall.

Example: Unstable Singularity ("When I die, Delete target unit.") dies in deployment with only its controller's other unit on the board: its trigger must target that unit, with no option to choose none, and deletes it.

Example: Shoreline Specter ("After combat, you may recall target ally. If you do, each opponent loses 2 life.") offers the decline beside its allies as its trigger goes on the stack. Declined, nothing is recalled and no opponent loses life.

Example: Shoreline Specter given a target recalls that ally and each opponent loses 2 life, with no further question as it resolves.

Example: Chombot ("You may move up to two counters from target unit onto another target unit") may be declined before its first target; once one is chosen, the second is required.

703. The Stack and Priority

703.1. The stack is "first in, last out". A new effect is put on top of the effects already there. When it is time to resolve, the top effect resolves first, so the effect put on last resolves first.

Example: Mycelial Mentor is played with Bloomcaster out. Bloomcaster's trigger goes on the stack above the Mentor, so its 1/1 is made before the Mentor arrives and the Mentor never sees it.

703.7. Deployment uses the stack, but each player has a stack of their own there, which only that player sees Digital client; no other player can respond to it or is made to wait on it. No player holds priority in deployment: a player cannot keep priority there or respond to an item on their own deployment stack. A player's plays still go on that stack, and it resolves on its own. See rule 507.

Example: In deployment a player plays a deploy-timing spell at their Earthbound Replicator; the spell goes on that player's own stack, so the Replicator can copy it.

Example: In deployment a player asks to keep priority as they play a card. The ask is refused: nobody can hold priority there.

704. Resolution and Fizzling

704.1. When an effect resolves, its instructions are carried out in the order printed, and a later instruction sees the results of an earlier one. The exception is target legality: it is judged once, as the effect begins to resolve (rule 704.5), so an earlier instruction cannot make a later instruction's target illegal. See rule 704.5.

Example: Finality ("Negate all other effects. Erase all cards in bins.") erases the cards it has just negated, because they are in bins by its second sentence.

705. Activated Abilities

705.1. An activated ability is written with a colon (":"). Everything before the colon is the cost of activating the ability; everything after it is the effect the ability has. See rule 109.2.

Example: Glook's "[once] Discard X cards: Glimpse 1, X times" — discarding X cards is the cost, and glimpsing X times is the effect.

  • Printed Manual p.41: colon is a cost that must be paid to activate the ability,

705.2. An activated ability may print a timing icon of its own. An ability marked {Battle} can be activated only during battle, and one marked {Deployment} only during deployment. The icon is checked when the ability is activated. See rules 109.2a, 109.2b.

Example: Grox's ability is marked {Battle}, so it cannot be activated during deployment.

Example: Cadaverous Cultivator's {Battle} ability is refused when activated outside battle, rather than doing nothing when it resolves.

706. Triggered Abilities

706.1. A triggered ability is an ability that happens when something else takes place. "When" and "Whenever" mark a triggered ability. A triggered ability can also happen at a stated time, such as "After combat" or "At the end of turn". See rule 109.3.

Example: Embermaw Fledgling's "after combat" ability creates an X/X unit after combat.

706.2. A triggered ability triggers at the moment its event happens, and whether it triggers is decided then (rule 109.3a). It is put on the stack afterwards, at one of the times this section gives, and its targets are chosen and its costs paid only as it is put on the stack. See rules 109.3a, 111.8.

Example: a "whenever I am dealt damage" ability triggers inside the combat damage step, but is put on the stack, and has its target chosen, after the step.

Example: the {Alluring} trigger chooses its target as it goes on the stack, and can then be negated.

Example: a spell played at Earthbound Replicator and then retargeted away still makes its copy.

706.11. {Alluring} and {Resonant} work as triggered abilities of the unit or source that has them. What they do is put on the stack, so it can be responded to and negated, and an effect that taxes triggered abilities applies to it. See rules 802, 111.10f.

Example: Crevice Lurker taxes the {Alluring} trigger, and declining the tax stops the lure.

Example: Containment Protocol negates an {Alluring} trigger waiting on the stack.

Example: a {Resonant} source's extra damage waits on the stack after combat as that source's ability, and can be negated.

706.12. Some triggered abilities choose a unit without targeting it, such as a Wraith's start-of-deployment ability choosing "an ally". The unit is chosen as the ability begins to resolve, from the units in play then. Several such abilities resolve one at a time, each choosing among the units still in play, so a unit an earlier one destroyed is not offered to a later one. One that finds no unit to choose fizzles. See rule 704.5c.

Example: three Wraith abilities and one 1/1 ally: only the first is offered the 1/1 and kills it; the other two put their counters on Wraiths still in play, and nothing fizzles.

Example: all three Wraith abilities are on the stack before the first one asks for its ally, and each asks only after the one before it has fully resolved.

Example: a Wraith with no other ally is its own only ally. Its ability chooses it without asking and it shrinks to 2/2; nothing fizzles.

Example: a 1/1 carrying two Wraith augments: the first ability kills it, and the second finds no ally in play and fizzles.

707. Static Abilities

707.1. A static ability states a change that its card continuously makes to the game for as long as the card is in play. See rule 109.4.

Example: Prickly Protector's "+1/+1 for each other ally" is counted again whenever its stats are read.

707.2. A static ability does not use the stack. It cannot be responded to or negated, and an effect that changes what abilities cost to activate or trigger does not apply to it.

Example: Crevice Lurker does not tax Tranquility's "spells cost [one] more"; Tranquility still adds exactly one.

Example: Aetherflux Golem's "I gain +2/+2" never goes on the stack, so Containment Protocol cannot negate it.

707.3. Only triggered abilities and activated abilities put anything on the stack. A triggered ability says "When" or "Whenever" or names a time such as "After combat"; {Alluring} and {Resonant} also work as triggered abilities; an activated ability is written with a colon. A sentence that states a standing fact ("I gain +2/+2", "Spells cost [one] more to play during battle") is a static ability, and a sentence that says "instead", "as" or "if" and names no target is a replacement effect. Neither goes on the stack, except that a replacement whose substitute names a target puts that substitute on the stack. See rules 708.1, 109.5a, 706.1, 706.11, 705.1, 708.2a.

708. Replacement and Prevention Effects

708.1. A replacement effect is an ability that changes an event as it happens, written "If … instead". It replaces the event, rather than triggering in response to it. See rule 109.5.

Example: Flux Resonator ("if one or more counters would be put on a unit by an allied source, put that many counters plus one instead") makes a counter put on an ally one more.

Sources and verification

  • Printed Manual p.41: and modify events as they happen, instead of triggering in response to events.

  • Example test 27-metal-b.test.ts::Flux Resonator: a counter you put on an allied unit becomes one more
  • Key effects.replacement.what

708.2. A replacement effect does not use the stack. It cannot be responded to, and an effect that negates triggered and activated effects (Containment Protocol) cannot stop it or undo what it did.

Example: Containment Protocol on the stack cannot negate Nullbringer's life-gain replacement.

708.4a If two or more replacement effects could apply to one event, they apply one at a time. Each applies at most once, to the event as the earlier ones left it, and only if that event still matches its own text; one that has applied does not apply again, so nothing loops. The player the event affects (the player who would be dealt the damage, the player whose rot it is, or the controller of the unit the counters would be put on) chooses the order in which they apply, except where rule 608.8c fixes it. When only one such effect applies, nothing is asked. Digital client

Example: two Oorblaks and combat damage that would be dealt to their controller: the first to apply takes all of it, and the other takes 0, because the damage is no longer being dealt to that player.

Example: the player who would be dealt the damage chooses which of two Oorblaks applies first, and that one takes it.

Example: two Counter Thieves: the counters the first redirects onto itself are still being placed on a unit, so the second, which has not applied, takes them; they end on the second to apply.

Example: the controller of the unit the counters were meant for chooses the order of two Counter Thieves; choosing the second to apply last puts the counters on it.

Example: two Counter Thieves do not pass the same counters back and forth: each applies once.

Example: two Automatons of Abundance turn one created token into three: 1, then 2, then 3.

Example: two Skittering Blights: the player whose rot it is chooses which one takes it as counters; the other has nothing left to replace.

709. Continuous Effects and Timestamps

709.1. A continuous effect changes the game for a period of time rather than once. It comes either from a static ability, and lasts as long as that ability is in play, only in its region; or from an effect that says how long it lasts, such as "until regroup". See rules 206.6, 113, 707.

Example: Sudden Bloom gives your units in its region +1/+1 until regroup, and the bonus is gone after regroup.

709.2. A continuous effect applies to a unit that enters play while the effect applies, from the moment it enters. The unit enters play already changed, so an ability that looks at the unit as it enters sees the changed unit. See rule 707.

Example: under Sandstone Defender ("Your other units gain +0/+2") a 1/1 enters as a 1/3, so Nectar Ridge Oracle ("When another ally with greater defense than power spawns, draw a card") draws.

Example: under Infernal Wispweaver a 0/1 Wisp enters as a 2/2, so Nectar Ridge Oracle does not draw.

Example: a unit that entered play under Transmogrifant has no attributes; when Transmogrifant leaves play it has them again.

Example: when Infernal Wispweaver leaves play, Wisps sacrifice themselves after combat again.

709.4. A unit's stats are worked out layer by layer, in the order of rule 206.4. Every effect in one layer applies before any effect in the next layer, whatever order the effects began in. Within one layer, effects apply in timestamp order (rule 113). See rules 206.4, 113.1.

Example: An effect that makes a unit base 4/4 applies over Apex Prime's copy effect whether the copy began before it or after it, because base stats are a later layer than the copy.

709.4b In layer 4, the stat-changing attributes apply one after the other. Those the unit has from its augment mods apply first, in the order the mods were attached Digital client; then the rest of its own attributes, its printed ones in type-line order and then those effects have given it; then those its column shares with it, front to back. So Tough augmented onto a Balanced unit has its defense doubled, then its stats balanced; Tough applied to a Balanced unit by an effect balances, then doubles; and a Tough unit attacking with a Balanced unit behind it is doubled, then balanced. See rule 802.

Example: Child of Aether (2/0, printed Balanced) augmented with Rampart Guardian (Tough) is doubled first (still 2/0), then balanced: a 2/2.

Example: The same Child of Aether given Tough by an effect is balanced first (2/2), then doubled: a 2/4.

710. Copies and Faces

710.1. A unit that becomes a copy of a card takes that card's name, printed stats, attributes and text in place of its own. The physical card does not change: in every zone other than play it is still its own card (rule 410.3a). See rules 201.5, 410.3a.

Example: a Borrower of Forms that copies a unit takes its name, its attributes and its text.

Example: a unit that is a copy dies and its own card goes to the bin, not the copied card.

710.7. An ability that gives a unit "all abilities" of other units (Ancient One) gives it everything in those units' text boxes, including the text their mods give them and the abilities effects have given them, but not their attributes, their name or their stats. The unit has the text only while the other units qualify, and loses it the moment they stop; as it dies, it still has the text of the units it was adjacent to, so their "when I die" abilities trigger for it. It gets nothing from a unit that has lost its abilities, and none of a unit's text that works only while that card is in another zone (such as its bin). Two Ancient Ones adjacent to each other each have the abilities of every unit adjacent to either of them. Each unit it has the text from gives it a use of its own: next to two units with the same [once] ability, it may use that ability twice.

Example: Ancient One has an adjacent ally's static ability, and loses it when the column breaks.

Example: an adjacent ally's attributes are not given to Ancient One.

Example: Ancient One keeps its own name and stats.

Example: Ancient One between two Jollyglops makes a 1/1 for each of them when it is dealt damage.

Example: Ancient One between two Debt Bleps has two activations.

Example: Two adjacent Ancient Ones both have the abilities of a unit adjacent to either of them.

Example: An Ancient One dying with Reforge the Dead's grant on it and on its two neighbours makes three Robots.

Example: An adjacent ally that has lost its abilities lends Ancient One nothing.

Example: Ancient One does not have the bin text of a neighbour in play.

Example: A dying Ancient One has the "when I die" text of the allies it stood beside.

711. Control Change

711.1. When a player gains control of a unit, the unit changes sides: it becomes that player's unit, an ally of that player's units and an enemy of its former controller's. Its owner does not change. See rules 102.4, 102.5, 102.7b.

Example: A stolen unit is recalled: it goes to the hand of the player who controls it.

Example: Its owner is unchanged.

712. Stripping and Suppression

712.1. Some effects make a unit lose all its attributes, all its abilities, or both ("loses all attributes and abilities"). While the unit has lost them, they do not apply. See rule 113.3.

Example: Monke makes other units lose all attributes and abilities during battle.

Sources and verification

  • Tests 27-metal-b.test.ts

712.1a Losing all abilities takes everything the unit's text does by itself: its triggered abilities, its activated abilities (which cannot be activated), its static abilities and cost changes, and its replacement effects, whether printed on it, given by its mods or granted to it. A unit that loses its abilities stops applying its static abilities at once, whether a one-time effect (Suppression Field) or a continuous one (Transmogrifant, Monke) took them; two continuous strips that each fall under the other are rule 712.5. See rule 712.5.

Example: a copy silenced by Suppression Field stops applying the static it copied.

Example: With Transmogrifant and Sandstone Defender in play, Sandstone Defender has lost its abilities, so a 1/1 token gets only Transmogrifant's +2/+2 and is a 3/3.

712.5. Two continuous strips whose sources each fall under the other do not both apply: the newer one applies, and the source of the older one loses its abilities, so the older strip does not apply. If the newer source leaves play, the older strip applies again. Where only one of the two sources falls under the other's strip, that source loses its abilities, even if it came into play later (rule 113.3a).

Example: With two Transmogrifants in play, a 1/1 token is a 3/3: only the newer Transmogrifant's +2/+2 applies. The older one gets the newer one's +2/+2 and has lost its abilities; when the newer one leaves play, the older one applies again.

Example: Two Monkes in battle: the newer Monke keeps its abilities, and the older one loses them.

Example: The Everywhere comes into play under its controller's Transmogrifant: it loses its abilities, so the card it names keeps its abilities.

713. State Checks

713.1. State checks are made by the game itself, at safe points. In a state check, every unit that should be dead dies, and every token that is in a zone where it cannot exist ceases to exist. See rules 713.2, 713.5.

Example: a lethally damaged unit and a dead unit token both go at the next safe point; the card reaches the bin, the token is erased, and a token recalled to a hand is erased from it.

Sources and verification
Owner callConfirmedverified in round 1 · verifier ran no tests · 2 gate test files
  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-10-06 — quoted from the retired ruling register: safe point — the engine's state-based check. The end of every action is a safe
  • Owner ruling adopted 2026-08-25 — quoted from the retired ruling register: to exist in all zones other than in play/stack whenever SBAs are checked.
  • Tests 380-no-action-ends-dead.test.ts, 427-cr-continuous-effects.test.ts
  • Example test 427-cr-continuous-effects.test.ts::cr:effects.state.what — at a safe point a lethally damaged unit dies, a dead unit token is erased instead of staying in the bin, and a recalled token is erased from the hand
  • Key effects.state.what

713.2. A unit dies in a state check if its defense is 0 or less, or if the damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its defense. See rules 112.5, 206.

Example: the turn's draw takes Dreadspawn Horror ("I gain -1/-1 for each card in your hand") to 0 defense, and it dies.

  • Example test 380-no-action-ends-dead.test.ts::CR 503.5: the turn draw that takes Dreadspawn Horror to 0 defense kills it at the turn flip
  • Key effects.state.lethal

713.3. The end of every action is a safe point, so no action ends with a unit standing that should have died: not a draw, a draft, a recycle or a resource activation. An action that is waiting on a player's decision has not ended and is not at a safe point; it is checked when the answer comes and the action finishes. The one exception is Constructed's draw phase, where drawing 4 and putting 2 back are judged as one step: a player's units are not checked while that player still has the 2 cards to put back. See rules 503.5, 503.5b, 112.8, 713.3a.

Example: in Constructed, Dreadspawn Horror with 3 cards in hand is still in play after the draw of 4, and dies once its controller has put 2 back (5 cards in hand).

Example: in Constructed, Dreadspawn Horror with 1 card in hand is a 4/2 after the draw phase and lives.

Example: Pestilent Titan attacks and its trigger puts a -1/-1 counter on each unit. A 1/1 token dies as soon as it gets its counter, before the next unit gets one.

Example: Rampart Guardian makes a unit Tough, then Reality Bender makes it Inverted, and it dies with no damage on it.

713.4a Pure does not change a unit's printed stats, so it does not by itself save a unit from a state-check death: a Pure 2/3 dealt 3 damage dies. But a Pure unit ignores its own other attributes, the stat-changing ones included (rule 802.25a), so a combination of its own attributes cannot kill it in a state check. See rule 802.

Example: A Pure 1/3 that is also Tough and Inverted ignores both, reads 1/3, and lives through the state check.

714. Last-Known State

714.1. A unit's last-known state is what it was at the instant it left play: its card and the face it showed, its controller, its region, its attributes (including those its column shared with it), its power and defense, and the formation it stood in. See rule 704.7.

Example: Deathglow Strider, sharing Piercing in a Good Whale column with a +1/+1 counter, is destroyed before its after-combat trigger resolves; the trigger remembers a 3/4 Piercing Deathglow Strider of its controller, in that region and formation.
